opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that drug design isn't one problem. It's a whole cascade of problems, and to build something that genuinely changes how we discover medicines, you need AI capabilities across that entire chain, not just one impressive model.

At the core, you have to understand the physical world of biology at the molecular level. That starts with structure: what does a protein look like, and critically, how does it interact with other molecules like small-molecule drugs, other proteins, and nucleic acids? AlphaFold showed what's possible for single protein structures. But for drug design you care about interactions, about how a candidate molecule actually binds to a target, how strongly, and what that does to the system. So one big capability is generalizable models of molecular interaction that work even on things they've never seen before.

But structure alone doesn't get you a drug. A good drug has to hit the right target with the right affinity, avoid hitting a bunch of other things, be absorbed by the body, not be toxic, and be makeable by chemists. Each of those is its own prediction problem, and historically each has been tackled with different, fairly narrow tools. What excites me is the idea of building models that capture enough of the underlying physics and chemistry that these properties start to fall out of one coherent understanding, rather than a patchwork of separate heuristics.

Then there's the generative and search side. Chemical space is astronomically large, so it isn't enough to score molecules someone hands you. You need systems that can propose new molecules, reason about tradeoffs, and navigate toward candidates that satisfy many constraints at once. That's where ideas from areas I've worked on before, like reinforcement learning and agents that learn through search and self-improvement, become really relevant. You want something closer to an agent doing design than a static predictor.

And finally, you have to close the loop with the real world. Models are only as useful as their ability to make predictions that hold up in the lab. So a big part of the capability isn't purely algorithmic. It's building the right feedback between computation and experiment, so the models get better and the scientists trust them enough to change what they actually do.

So when I put it all together, the ambition is a general drug design engine: something that can take a new target, even one considered undruggable, and reliably help design molecules against it much faster and with a much higher success rate than today. We're not fully there yet, but the pieces are coming together faster than I think most people expect.

r001.rationale: The response describes several capabilities across the drug-design process, but gives no roughly half-dozen count or AlphaFold-like framing.

r002.rationale: It says molecular-interaction models should generalize to things they have never seen and describes applying the engine to a new target.

r003.rationale: It mentions interactions with small molecules, proteins, and nucleic acids, but does not state that Isomorphic Labs' models apply across multiple drug modalities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, there are really three layers of capability you need, and they build on each other.

The first is prediction. You need models that genuinely understand the structure and behavior of biological molecules, so proteins, small molecules, nucleic acids, and crucially how they interact. That's where something like AlphaFold 3 sits. It's not just folding a protein anymore, it's predicting how a drug-like molecule sits in a binding pocket, what the complex looks like, and doing that across the whole of biochemistry rather than one narrow slice. If you can't predict, you can't design, because design is fundamentally a search over a space where you need to evaluate candidates without synthesizing each one.

The second layer is generation. Once you have a model that can score or predict, you want to invert it. Rather than asking "what does this molecule do," you ask "give me a molecule that does this." That means generative models over chemical space that are conditioned on the structure, on the target, on the properties you care about. And the space is astronomically large, something like ten to the sixty plausible drug-like molecules, so you really need the generative model and the predictive model to be working together, with the predictor acting as the critic.

The third layer, and this is where my background in reinforcement learning and agents comes in, is the design loop itself. Drug design isn't a single prediction. It's a long sequence of decisions under uncertainty, where you have multiple competing objectives: potency, selectivity, solubility, toxicity, how it behaves in the body. Humans do this today through medicinal chemistry intuition and iterative cycles that take months. We want an engine that can reason over that trade-off landscape, propose, evaluate, update, and do it at a speed and breadth no human team could.

What's exciting is that the lessons from AlphaGo and from the broader Deepmind program really carry over. You have a world model, you have a policy for exploring, and you have feedback. The difference is that in biology the feedback is expensive and noisy, so a huge part of the engineering is about being data efficient and knowing when to trust the model versus when to go to the lab.

And the thing I'd emphasize is that none of these layers is static. We're training foundation models of biology, but we're also shaping how data comes back from experiments so the next version is better. That flywheel is really the engine.

r001.rationale: The response describes three capability layers and mentions AlphaFold 3, but never says the engine requires roughly half a dozen AlphaFold-like capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says the models should cover interactions across “the whole of biochemistry rather than one narrow slice,” communicating broad applicability across biological targets.

r003.rationale: The response names several types of biological molecules, but does not state that Isomorphic’s models are applicable across multiple drug modalities.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as a collection of capabilities that have to come together. Understanding the structure of a protein is incredibly useful, but it’s one piece of the problem. For drug design, you want to understand how molecules interact, how changing a molecule changes that interaction, and ultimately what that means for the biological system you’re trying to influence.

Then you need to move from prediction to design. Can you generate a molecule that has the properties you want? And that’s a very challenging problem because you’re optimizing for many things simultaneously. Binding to the right target matters, but so do selectivity, safety, and whether the molecule can get to where it needs to act in the body.

The other crucial capability is learning from experiments. You want your models to help choose which experiments to run, and then use the results to improve the next round of predictions and designs. So I wouldn’t frame it as one model that solves drug discovery. It’s building a system where molecular understanding, generative design, and experimental feedback reinforce one another.

r001.rationale: Describes several capabilities but does not state that roughly half a dozen AlphaFold-like capabilities are required.

r002.rationale: Mentions designing for the right target, but does not say the models generalize across biological targets.

r003.rationale: Does not report that the models apply across multiple drug modalities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the scientific problem: what would we need to predict to design a molecule that becomes a really effective medicine? Understanding the structure of a protein is an incredibly important part of that, but it’s one part. You also need to understand how a molecule interacts with that protein, how it changes its function, and how that molecule will behave in the body.

So I don’t think of it as one prediction task. You need a collection of capabilities that come together into a design engine. You need predictive models that can tell you whether an idea is promising, generative models that can propose new molecules, and a way of reasoning about which experiment would be most useful to do next.

And the experimental loop is crucial. You design something, you make it, you test it, and you use what you learn to improve the next round. The exciting opportunity is to make that whole loop much more powerful with AI—to move from predicting properties of molecules to actually helping us discover better medicines.

r002.rationale: It does not state that the models generalize across biological targets.

r003.rationale: It does not report applicability across multiple drug modalities.
